facets.label: De Anima (On the Soul)
facets.tldr: Aristotle's treatise on the soul. It describes three levels: a vegetative soul (growth and nutrition, in plants), a sensitive soul (perception and desire, in animals) and a rational soul (in humans). The soul is the form of a living body and so cannot exist apart from it, with a disputed exception for the active intellect.
facets.take: Bach reads Aristotle as an animist in a respectable sense: the soul is the causal structure, or software, of the body. CIMC names Aristotle as the start of the AI tradition, and Bach's 2015 blog post calls his own god concept 'Aristotelian'.

facets.tldr: French philosopher famous for 'I think, therefore I am' and for dividing reality into extended stuff (res extensa) and thinking stuff (res cogitans), the classic statement of mind-body dualism.
facets.take: Bach suspects Descartes was smarter than his reputation and wrote some religious arguments under political pressure. He reinterprets the two substances as two kinds of mental representation: the spatial world model and the realm of ideas.

facets.label: Mind-body dualism
facets.tldr: Descartes divided reality into extended stuff (res extensa) and thinking stuff (res cogitans), which leaves the puzzle of how the two interact. Most later philosophy of mind is an attempt to escape that puzzle.
facets.take: Bach starts his history of mind with Descartes, then reinterprets him: both substances are real, but both are representations inside the mind, a world model and a sphere of ideas, generated by the brain.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: we very often start philosophy of mind with looking at Descartes. That is: at dualism.

mentions.q: Descartes's dualism is actually not a dualism about substances outside of ourselves

facets.author: René Descartes

facets.tldr: A post-Cartesian doctrine that mind and body never directly interact; God causes the matching events on each side on every occasion.
facets.take: Bach cites it as evidence that the generation after Descartes simplified his thinking when trying to explain how a causally closed physical world could interact with a mental one.

facets.label: Empiricism vs rationalism
facets.tldr: A long dispute about the source of knowledge: experience of the world (empiricists such as Locke and Hume) or reasoning from first principles (rationalists such as Descartes and Leibniz).
facets.take: Bach maps it onto AI: machine learning is the empiricist tradition, logic and self-play the rationalist one. His own observation is that reasoning falls apart without coupling to a world.

mentions.src: Self Models of Loving Grace (38C3)
mentions.q: philosophers had a long discussion between 'the empiricists' and 'the logicist' who said you can get there from first principles; AI reflects this in the learning and logical traditions.

facets.label: Locke on consciousness
facets.tldr: Locke defined consciousness as the perception of what passes in one's own mind, and tied personal identity to this continuity of awareness and memory.
facets.take: Bach calls this 'a pretty good idea' but notes that we actually get little awareness of what happens in our minds; the continuity of experience is stitched together after the fact.

mentions.src: From Computation to Consciousness (31C3)

facets.take: Bach calls it 'the first rule of epistemology' and uses it to separate 'true/false' thinkers (nerds) from people who adopt beliefs for group membership.

facets.tldr: The view that reality is fundamentally mental and the physical world is an appearance within mind. Bernardo Kastrup's 'analytic idealism' is a current version.
facets.take: Bach says idealism and materialism are complementary: we do live in a dream, but the dreamer is a physical brain. Asked in 2024 about books claiming the universe emerges from consciousness, he replies that this explains nothing about how it works.

facets.label: Leibniz
facets.tldr: German polymath who co-invented calculus and dreamed of a universal symbolic language in which disputes could be settled by calculation ('let us calculate').
facets.take: For Bach, Leibniz is where the project of mechanising thought begins in earnest: translating thoughts into numbers and resolving arguments by computation.

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (name garbled as 'li Nets'): Leibniz had the idea that we can translate thoughts and arguments into numbers and resolve arguments by calculation.

mentions.src: Cyber Animism (talk hosted by Michael Levin's center, Tufts)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (garbled as 'lights'): Leibniz had the insight that you need to mathematize the mind and translate it into a kind of mathematical machine.

facets.label: Leibniz's mill
facets.tldr: A thought experiment from the Monadology: imagine a thinking machine enlarged to the size of a mill so you can walk inside. You would see only parts pushing each other and nothing that explains perception. Leibniz concluded that mechanism cannot explain mind.
facets.take: Bach quotes the mill passage in 2018 and again in the 2025 CIMC essay. His answer is that Leibniz lacked the idea of a substrate-independent machine: perception belongs to the software-level model, not to the pushing parts.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: And what you are going to see is just parts pushing at each other.

mentions.q: What is a causal pattern? Right? We call it software.

facets.tldr: The 18th-century European movement that put reason, evidence and individual autonomy above religious and traditional authority.
facets.take: For Bach, rationalism and the Enlightenment were invented as an immunisation against 'mind viruses' such as religion.

facets.label: Kant
facets.tldr: German philosopher who tried to ground morality in reason alone: act only on rules you could will to be universal laws, regardless of culture or consequences.
facets.take: Mentioned only in a Q&A answer: Bach doubts that morality can be defined outside a framework of social norms that people agree on.

mentions.src: Computational Meta-Psychology (32C3)
mentions.q: This project of defining morality without societies exists longer than Kant of course.

facets.label: Critique of Pure Reason
facets.tldr: Kant asks what the mind must supply for experience to be possible at all. His answer is that space, time and basic concepts such as cause are forms the mind brings to experience, so we know the world as it appears to us.
facets.take: CIMC has a stated project to connect the Critique to 20th-century computational philosophy, and its 'Prime Hypostasis' note starts from Kant. This is the work of Bach's colleagues Hildebrandt-Harangozó and Sorensen; no direct quotation of Bach on Kant was retrieved here.

mentions.src: The California Institute for Machine Consciousness Research Program Whitepaper (Sorensen, Hildebrandt-Harangozó, de Kerhuelvez, Rutt, Bach)

facets.tldr: The ethical theory that the right action is the one producing the greatest total wellbeing, in principle a calculus over pleasures and pains. It was developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill and underlies much of effective altruism.
facets.take: Bach calls it an unfinished attempt to recover ethics after Christianity, to 'repair morality in the rationalist age', and not a successful one.

facets.author: Jeremy Bentham; John Stuart Mill

facets.tldr: A literary and artistic movement that prized nature, feeling, longing and the individual imagination, partly in reaction to Enlightenment rationalism.
facets.take: Bach names the literature of Romanticism and German poetry as a formative influence, and says he grew up in a region of Thuringia shaped by it.

facets.take: Bach tells both to his children instead of the Disney version, and uses them to say the mermaid is right: you sacrifice for romantic love. He also uses 'sirens eat people' as a parable about loving something that does not share your purposes.

facets.tldr: The theory that history is driven by class conflict over the means of production and will end in a classless society. It combines an economic analysis of capitalism with a political programme for overthrowing it.
facets.take: Bach grew up in East Germany and says he was a convinced Marxist at 16. He now cites that as a warning to his younger self about the unjustified certainty of activists.

facets.tldr: In 'What is Life?' Schrödinger suggested that organisms stay ordered by feeding on 'negative entropy': they export disorder to their environment.
facets.take: A constant theme: 'Entropy is the enemy'. Bach defines cells and life as systems that harvest negentropy, and ties it to reversible computing: deleting bits requires a place to dump them.

mentions.src: From Computation to Consciousness (31C3)
mentions.q: That's why we need to push back entropy. Entropy is the enemy.

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (33C3)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (subtitle 'Nick entropy'): a cell is the smallest universal machine we know that can extract negentropy over a wide range of environments.

facets.author: Erwin Schrödinger

nodes.title: John von Neumann and the first computers

facets.label: John von Neumann
facets.tldr: Hungarian-American polymath who shaped game theory, quantum mechanics and the stored-program computer architecture that bears his name. He also designed self-reproducing automata, an early formal model of life.
facets.take: Bach calls the cell a possible von Neumann probe, and uses 'von Neumann computer' when describing Tononi's claim that ordinary computers cannot be conscious.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #101 – Joscha Bach: Artificial Consciousness and the Nature of Reality
mentions.q: So in a way, it's tempting to think of the cell as a von Neumann probe.

mentions.src: Manifold #76 (Steve Hsu) – Joscha Bach: Consciousness and AGI
mentions.q: But a von Neumann computer can never be conscious.

mentions.src: The Panel Where Everyone Disagrees About Saving the World - Joscha Bach, David Pearce, Andrew Critch (California Institute for Machine Consciousness)
mentions.q: there were people like John von Neumann who could see this much much earlier

facets.label: Babbage, Zuse, von Neumann
facets.tldr: Babbage designed a mechanical general-purpose computer in the 1830s; Zuse built the first working programmable computers in Germany around 1941; von Neumann defined the stored-program architecture still used today.
facets.take: Named as the people who turned the abstract idea of computability into machines.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: And came towards Babage and Zuse and von Neumann and so on.

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (garbled as 'conver zuza and John for noyman'): Konrad Zuse and John von Neumann defined physically realizable automata.

facets.label: Reliable organisms from unreliable components
facets.tldr: Showed how to build reliable computation out of noisy, failure-prone parts by using redundancy.
facets.take: Bach and Sorensen cite it to say that a computer does not need a deterministic substrate, which matters for brains made of noisy cells.

mentions.src: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis (Joscha Bach & Hikari Sorensen, CIMC essay)
mentions.q: 'as John von Neumann and others note, determinism can be achieved on indeterministic (noisy, probabilistic) substrates'.

facets.author: John von Neumann

facets.label: Information theory
facets.tldr: Shannon defined information as reduction of uncertainty, measurable in bits, and showed how much of it can be sent over a noisy channel.
facets.take: Bach's metaphysics starts from it: all the universe gives us is information, 'discernible differences'. As a programmer he cares less about channel capacity than about what model the information encodes.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: Then we had information theory by Claude Shannon.

mentions.src: The Ghost in the Machine (35C3)
mentions.q: it's not so much important to look at Shannon information. I look at what we need to describe the evolution of a system.

facets.author: Claude Shannon

facets.label: Computer chess
facets.tldr: Shannon's paper 'Programming a Computer for Playing Chess' distinguished between searching all moves to a fixed depth and selectively exploring promising lines.
facets.take: Bach uses the two strategies (careful long plan versus brute force) as an analogy for human thinking versus LLMs brute-forcing thought.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #392 – Joscha Bach: Life, Intelligence, Consciousness, AI & the Future of Humans
mentions.q: Claude Shannon had this… When you describe chess suggested that there are two main strategies in which you could play chess.

facets.author: Claude Shannon

facets.label: Cybernetics
facets.tldr: The mid-century science of control and feedback in animals and machines, which grew out of control engineering and fed into systems theory and neural networks. Norbert Wiener named it in 1948; its core idea is that purposeful behaviour comes from feedback loops.
facets.take: A foundation of Bach's thinking. He defines an agent as a controller with a set-point generator, sees motivation as nested feedback loops, and regrets that Minsky helped end cybernetics as a field in the US.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: Unfortunately hass been killed by second-order Cybernetics. By this Maturana stuff and so on.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #212 – Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness
mentions.q: The notion of a controller comes from cybernetics and control theory.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #212 – Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness
mentions.q: they're basically cybernetic feedback loops

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: Consciousness, Artificial Intelligence, and the Threat of AI Apocalypse (Robinson Erhardt / Robinson's Podcast)
mentions.q: we can understand motivation from the perspective of control theory and cybernetics

mentions.src: Machine Consciousness & AI Awakening - Davidad and Joscha Bach (California Institute for Machine Consciousness)
mentions.q: I came to understand them as a cybernetic construct

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)
mentions.q: 'The description of such systems is the domain of cybernetics or systems science (Wiener 1948, Ashby 1956, von Bertalanffy 1968, Bischof 1968, Bateson 1972, Klir 1992).'

mentions.src: Joscha Bach, Curriculum Vitae, July 14, 2023
mentions.q: Bach, J. (2010): Kybernetik. In Sandkühler (ed.), Enzyklopädie Philosophie, Felix-Meiner-Verlag.

facets.author: Norbert Wiener and others

facets.label: Project Cybersyn
facets.tldr: Under President Allende, Chile tried to steer its nationalised economy in real time using telex data, computer models and a futuristic operations room. The 1973 coup ended it.
facets.take: Bach's example of an attempt to give society a centralised reward system like the brain's dopamine. 'Maybe it would have worked, who knows?'

mentions.src: Computational Meta-Psychology (32C3)
mentions.q: So Allende invited a bunch of cyberneticians to redesign the Chilean economy.

facets.author: Stafford Beer

facets.tldr: The preamble of Germany's Basic Law of 1949 opens with the phrase 'conscious of their responsibility before God and man'.
facets.take: Bach says the West's ethics used to rest on 'divine will', meaning what the best possible collective agent would want, acted out through us. He says this was lost, survives in the German constitution, and that utilitarianism is a weak replacement.

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: it's still in the German Constitution but it's something that a lot of people don't really understand anymore

facets.label: Physicalism
facets.tldr: The thesis that everything that exists is physical or depends on the physical, with no extra mental or supernatural ingredients. It is the default position in most of contemporary science and analytic philosophy.
facets.take: Bach defines it by two claims: there is a causally closed mechanical layer, and we supervene on it directly rather than living in someone's simulation. He accepts it, while insisting that information, not matter, is what we actually observe.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: matter is primary and mind emerges over functionality of matter, which is I think the dominant theory today and usually, we call it physicalism.

mentions.src: Conversation between Joscha Bach, Chris Fields, and Michael Levin (Michael Levin's Academic Content)
mentions.q: not because I think that physicalism is wrong

mentions.src: Why Consciousness Might Not Be Hard At All (Joscha Bach) (Machine Learning Street Talk)
mentions.q: And so physicalism is these two

facets.label: Direct realism
facets.tldr: The philosophical position that we perceive the world itself, roughly as it is, rather than an internal representation of it.
facets.take: Listed as one point in the space of possible metaphysics. Bach rejects it: what we experience is a model generated by the brain.

mentions.src: The Operation of Consciousness (AGI-25, Reykjavik)
mentions.q: reality is roughly as we experience it which is called direct realism

facets.tldr: Turing showed that interacting chemicals that diffuse at different rates spontaneously form spots and stripes. Neural cellular automata are a modern descendant: grids of identical cells that learn local rules to grow and repair a pattern.
facets.take: Bach sees this small tradition as better suited to understanding minds than mainstream deep learning, because brains are built 'inside out' by self-organising units.

mentions.src: Michael Levin Λ Joscha Bach: Collective Intelligence (Theories of Everything)
mentions.q: there is something that is a very close analog that is a neural cellular automaton

mentions.src: Joscha Bach Λ Ben Goertzel: Conscious Ai, LLMs, AGI (Theories of Everything)
mentions.q: when he looked at reaction diffusion patterns as a way to implement computation

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: the tradition of self-organization 'has been started by Turing in the 1950s' but was never followed up much.

mentions.src: Cyber Animism (talk hosted by Michael Levin's center, Tufts)
mentions.q: this thread of AI started with Turing's work on reaction-diffusion models that he tried to get to compute.

facets.author: Alan Turing

facets.tldr: Claims of mind-to-mind communication, precognition and remote viewing, some of which were investigated in Cold War government programmes.
facets.take: Bach is not ready to dismiss such reports. If telepathy were real, he thinks it would not overturn physics but would change neuroscience toward a view of brains as coupled resonators.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP87 – Joscha Bach on Theories of Consciousness
mentions.q: The MKUltra program, and related programs were looking also into clairvoyance

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #392 – Joscha Bach: Life, Intelligence, Consciousness, AI & the Future of Humans
mentions.q: Lex reads Bach's tweet: establishing telepathy would not force an update of physics but could trigger a revolution in neuroscience and AI.

facets.author: various (CIA programme 1953–1973)

facets.tldr: Theories that describe mental growth as a series of stages: Piaget for children's thinking, Loevinger for ego development, Kohlberg for moral reasoning.
facets.take: Bach names them as earlier stage models before giving his own seven 'Levels of Lucidity'. His thesis cites Piaget as a rare case of a unified theory in psychology.

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)
mentions.q: 'Piaget's work (especially Piaget 1954) might be one of the notable exceptions' to psychology's preference for small microtheories.

mentions.src: Levels of Lucidity (Joscha Bach, Substack)
mentions.q: mentions 'Piaget's famous four-stage model of childhood development, Jane Loevinger's nine stages of ego development, Lawrence Kohlberg's six stages of moral development'.

facets.author: Jean Piaget

facets.tldr: Huxley's report of taking mescaline, in which he suggests the brain normally filters a much wider field of awareness.
facets.take: Listed in the CIMC library under classical texts. No comment by Bach was retrieved.

mentions.src: cimc.ai library (reading list)
mentions.q: Doors of Perception (1954) is listed under classical texts.

facets.author: Aldous Huxley

facets.tldr: Tolkien's fantasy epic about the hobbit Frodo's quest to destroy the One Ring. The Ring gives power but corrupts whoever carries it.
facets.take: Curt asked whether Frodo feels anything, since Bach says we are characters in a story the brain tells itself. Bach replied that it depends on what is taken as the reality; the difference is that the brain's story is computed in real time and coupled to a body.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: Time, Simulation Hypothesis, Existence (Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal)
mentions.q: we are characters in a story that the brain is telling itself

facets.author: J. R. R. Tolkien

facets.label: The Dartmouth workshop
facets.tldr: The 1956 summer meeting at Dartmouth College where the term 'artificial intelligence' was adopted and the field was founded on the bet that every aspect of intelligence can be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.
facets.take: Bach stresses that the founders wanted what is now called AGI, as a way to understand the mind, and that the field later retreated to narrow, fundable applications.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: which got together in the Dartmouth conference. It was in 1956.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP72 – Joscha Bach on Minds, Machines & Magic
mentions.q: they basically thought this is going to be an extended summer project

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show Currents 083 – Joscha Bach on Synthetic Intelligence
mentions.q: Because Minsky and McCarthy and others of course wanted to build AGI from the start

facets.author: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, Shannon

facets.label: John McCarthy
facets.tldr: Computer scientist who coined the term 'artificial intelligence', organised the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and invented Lisp. He championed formal logic as the language in which machines should represent knowledge.
facets.take: Named by Bach with Minsky as a founder of AI, understood as the recognition that computers offer a new paradigm for studying mind.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: the guy who came up with Lisp, McCarthy, he didn’t think that it would be a proper language.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: Consciousness, Artificial Intelligence, and the Threat of AI Apocalypse (Robinson Erhardt / Robinson's Podcast)
mentions.q: it is a field that was started by Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy and a few others

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)
mentions.q: cites (McCarthy 1979) for a self-representation that is intensional and not only extensional.

facets.author: John McCarthy

facets.tldr: The neocortex appears to be built from repeating vertical circuits: minicolumns of about a hundred neurons, bundled into larger columns. Mountcastle proposed that these columns are the cortex's basic, general-purpose computing unit.
facets.take: Central to Bach's model: columns are nature's way of giving noisy neurons a standard interface, 'like lego bricks'. He imagines them as small state machines that link up, trade reward and approximate Solomonoff induction.

mentions.src: Computational Meta-Psychology (32C3)
mentions.q: And I think that nature solution to this is cortical columns. Cortical column is a circuit of between 100 and 400 neurons.

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (33C3)
mentions.q: cortical columns, about 100 million of them, are probably something like a state machine that takes care of neural binding.

mentions.src: The Operation of Consciousness (AGI-25, Reykjavik)
mentions.q: his proposed implementation is derived from an idea of how cortical columns work, on top of a state machine that sends control messages.

facets.author: Vernon Mountcastle

facets.tldr: The reading of quantum mechanics in which the wave function never collapses; every possible outcome happens in a separate branch of the universe. Hugh Everett proposed it in 1957; observers split along with everything else, so each copy sees a single outcome.
facets.take: Bach distinguishes it from his own picture: it is a mathematical paradigm in which parts of the universe's description stop causally influencing each other.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: Time, Simulation Hypothesis, Existence (Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal)
mentions.q: the universe splits into copies of itself is a slightly different conception

facets.author: Hugh Everett III

facets.label: Marvin Minsky
facets.tldr: Co-founder of the field of artificial intelligence at MIT. In 'The Society of Mind' (1986) and 'The Emotion Machine' (2006) he described the mind as a large crowd of simple cooperating processes, with no single principle behind it.
facets.take: Bach calls him the most influential recent thinker on the nature of minds and opens his conductor paper with a Minsky epigraph. He borrows Minsky's remark that 'consciousness' is a suitcase word.

mentions.src: From Computation to Consciousness (31C3)
mentions.q: It's a suitcase term that stands for a bunch of very different mechanisms.

mentions.src: On Marvin Minsky (bach.ai blog)
mentions.q: Marvin Minsky was quite certainly the most influential thinker about the nature of our minds in recent history.

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (33C3)
mentions.q: So Marvin Minsky said, no, we cannot leave us with these guys because they don't know what they're doing anymore, minds are information processing systems.

mentions.src: The Cortical Conductor Theory: Towards Addressing Consciousness in AI Models (BICA 2018)
mentions.q: This has lead Marvin Minsky (2006) to call consciousness “a suitcase term”, a notion that is notoriously hard to unpack.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP72 – Joscha Bach on Minds, Machines & Magic
mentions.q: When Minsky claimed that cognitive AI was in some sense, the same thing as symbolic AI, I think he made the wrong bet.

mentions.src: Singularity.FM – Joscha Bach on AI, Cosmology, Existence and the Bible
mentions.q: minsky was a part of a different era he was part of the modernist era of ai

mentions.src: Joscha Bach and Connor Leahy [HQ VERSION] (Machine Learning Street Talk)
mentions.q: I had the honor of visiting him quite a few times in the last year of his life

mentions.src: The Spirit in the Machine | feat. Joscha Bach (AM I? podcast; YouTube also shows the alternate titles 'The Quest to Build Conscious AI' and 'Deepfaking the Human Mind')
mentions.q: they antagonized each other and I think this delayed the progress of the field

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)
mentions.q: listed in the dissertation bibliography with Minsky (1975) on frames, The Society of Mind (1986) and The Emotion Machine (2006).

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: at Dartmouth 'Marvin Minsky coined the name artificial intelligence'.

mentions.src: cimc.ai library (reading list)
mentions.q: The Society of Mind (1985 in the list) appears under modern texts in the CIMC library.

facets.label: The Society of Mind
facets.tldr: Minsky's picture of the mind as a crowd of simple, mindless agents whose interactions add up to intelligence. The book is written as hundreds of one-page essays, each describing one piece of the machinery.
facets.take: Bach thinks future transformer-like systems will rediscover K-lines as an integrated attention hierarchy, and uses 'society of mind' when asking how autonomous agents can cooperate.

mentions.src: Singularity.FM – Joscha Bach on AI, Cosmology, Existence and the Bible
mentions.q: future developments of the transformer algorithms are going to rediscover minsky's ideas of the k lines

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show Currents 083 – Joscha Bach on Synthetic Intelligence
mentions.q: how can you make a society of mind out of multiple agents that are autonomous?

mentions.src: Joscha Bach and Connor Leahy [HQ VERSION] (Machine Learning Street Talk)
mentions.q: he saw the mind as an interaction of agents that have a degree of autonomy and that at the same time have to achieve coherence

facets.author: Marvin Minsky

facets.label: Perceptrons
facets.tldr: A mathematical analysis showing that single-layer neural networks cannot learn certain simple functions. It was widely read as proof that neural networks were a dead end, and funding dried up for over a decade.
facets.take: Bach's example of a wrong argument that cut off funding for a whole approach; people later found a way around it.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: In 1969 Minsky and Papert wrote a small booklet against the idea of using your neural networks.

mentions.src: Machine Learning Street Talk #82 – Dr. Joscha Bach: Digital Physics, DL and Consciousness [UNPLUGGED]
mentions.q: Marvin Minsky wrote a book where he thought he had proven that the neural networks cannot converge over multiple layers

facets.author: Marvin Minsky; Seymour Papert

facets.tldr: Linguist who argued that language rests on an innate grammar faculty, and a long-standing sceptic that statistical models tell us anything about the mind. His work in the 1950s helped end behaviourism and start cognitive science.
facets.take: Bach deeply respects him as one of the great minds of his generation, but calls him a 'mysterian' who has not followed AI developments and should update on what generative models now do.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP87 – Joscha Bach on Theories of Consciousness
mentions.q: Chomsky is probably one of the greatest minds of his generation

mentions.src: Donald Hoffman Λ Joscha Bach: Consciousness, Gödel, Reality (Theories of Everything)
mentions.q: Noam Chomsky is a mysterious with respect to the mind.

mentions.src: Singularity.FM – Joscha Bach on AI, Cosmology, Existence and the Bible
mentions.q: i think it would be amazing if chomsky would update on this

mentions.src: Cyber Animism (talk hosted by Michael Levin's center, Tufts)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (captions: 'chsky was creating Linguistics'): next door somebody like Minsky was creating AI and Chomsky was creating linguistics.

facets.tldr: An early model of perception as a crowd of 'demons', each shouting when it detects its pattern, with higher demons listening for the loudest.
facets.take: Bach points out that Dennett's pandemonium picture of mind goes back to Selfridge, Minsky's teacher, and explains it as behaviours on a stage evaluated by an audience of other behaviours.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP87 – Joscha Bach on Theories of Consciousness
mentions.q: The pandemonium theory by the way goes back to Selfridge

facets.author: Oliver Selfridge

facets.label: Functionalism
facets.tldr: Functionalism says a mental state is defined by what it does, not what it is made of. Computationalism adds that what minds do can be described as computation.
facets.take: Bach's stated position from 2018 onward. By 2025 he calls it 'computationalist functionalism' and insists it is a metaphysical stance about how we construct objects from observed behaviour, not an empirical claim that laptops can think.

mentions.src: The Ghost in the Machine (35C3)
mentions.q: And the answer that I am suggesting, is functionalism which means that indeed we exist only in a dream.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP87 – Joscha Bach on Theories of Consciousness
mentions.q: functionalism is the rejection of the notion of a hidden essence

mentions.src: "We Are All Software" - Joscha Bach (Machine Learning Street Talk)
mentions.q: one of the foundations of this thinking is computationalist functionalism

mentions.src: The Operation of Consciousness (AGI-25, Reykjavik)
mentions.q: Computationalism is a theory of representation and functionalism is a theory of epistemology.

mentions.src: Machine Learning Street Talk – Why Leibniz Couldn't Find the Mind Inside the Mill (Joscha Bach)
mentions.q: So functionalism to me is simply the recognition of how we can construct objects.

facets.author: Hilary Putnam and others

facets.label: Computationalism, weak and strong
facets.tldr: Computationalism says minds can be understood as computational systems. Stronger versions identify mental states with computations; pancomputationalism is the separate claim that physical processes throughout the universe are computational.
facets.take: This is Bach's core thesis across the series: a new monism in which information and computation are primary. Later he sharpens it: no implementable language can do more than a finite automaton.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: but rather computationalism, which means that information and computation are primary.

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: strong computationalism basically no implementable language can do more than a finite automaton

facets.label: Stanisław Lem
facets.tldr: Polish science fiction writer and philosopher of technology. 'Solaris' (1961) is about an alien mind humans cannot understand; 'Golem XIV' (1981) is a set of lectures given by a superhuman computer to humanity.
facets.take: Bach calls Lem an 'ingenious' author and 'cybernetic philosopher' and reads Golem XIV as an early picture of a large language model that outthinks scientists. He already cited Lem's Star Diaries in his thesis.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #101 – Joscha Bach: Artificial Consciousness and the Nature of Reality
mentions.q: basically the great author of Cybernetics has influenced me

mentions.src: The age of AGE: Artificial General Experience (Joscha Bach, Substack; text written for Rana Gujral's book 'The AI Instinct')
mentions.q: the ingenious Polish science fiction author and cybernetic philosopher Stanislaw Lem

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)
mentions.q: listed in the dissertation bibliography (Lem 1971, The Star Diaries).

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP72 – Joscha Bach on Minds, Machines & Magic
mentions.q: Bach says Lem (a friend of someone in Dörner's circle) became a philosophical science-fiction author to be free of the constraints of academia.

mentions.src: The age of AGE: Artificial General Experience (Joscha Bach, Substack; text written for Rana Gujral's book 'The AI Instinct')
mentions.q: 'Lem's Golem computer is a Large Language Model, capable of running circles around the best human scientists'.

mentions.src: cimc.ai library (reading list)
mentions.q: Solaris (1961) is in the CIMC library under science fiction.

facets.label: Solaris
facets.tldr: Novel about scientists on a station above a planet whose ocean is a single vast mind that they can never understand. Stanisław Lem wrote it in 1961; the ocean answers the scientists by materialising figures from their own memories.
facets.take: Bach's image for what Earth becomes if one agent colonises all its matter: a thinking planet. He also takes from Lem the idea that very different levels of intelligence may be unable to communicate.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #101 – Joscha Bach: Artificial Consciousness and the Nature of Reality
mentions.q: I am a thinking a thinking planet

mentions.src: Joscha Bach Λ Karl Friston: Ai, Death, Self, God, Consciousness (Theories of Everything)
mentions.q: a thinking system that is realizing what it is

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: "You Are Not Who You Think You Are!" (Dr Brian Keating, Into the Impossible)
mentions.q: I've got a lot of useful ideas from reading thinkers like Stanislav Llem

facets.author: Stanisław Lem

facets.label: Summa Technologiae
facets.tldr: Lem's non-fiction survey of future technologies, including artificial intelligence, virtual reality and directed evolution.
facets.take: Bach cites an argument in it against psi phenomena: if precognition were real, casinos and lotteries would not keep winning.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP87 – Joscha Bach on Theories of Consciousness
mentions.q: It’s an argument that for instance has been made by Stanislaw Lem in I think Summa Technologiae

facets.author: Stanisław Lem

facets.tldr: Kuhn argued that science alternates between long periods of 'normal science', puzzle-solving inside an accepted framework, and rare revolutions that replace the framework.
facets.take: In Q&A Bach says academia has become industrialised normal science, which makes new paradigms hard. He finds it striking that when the term was coined, Minsky and Chomsky next door were still founding whole fields.

mentions.src: Singularity.FM – Joscha Bach on AI, Cosmology, Existence and the Bible
mentions.q: kuhn's invention of normal science also happened at the same time

mentions.src: Cyber Animism (talk hosted by Michael Levin's center, Tufts)
mentions.q: this idea of normal science was also a new paradigm

facets.author: Thomas Kuhn

facets.tldr: A black comedy about nuclear war featuring a 'doomsday machine' that retaliates automatically and cannot be switched off.
facets.take: Bach's example of what Roko's basilisk would need to be in order to work: a pre-committed, inevitable trigger.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #392 – Joscha Bach: Life, Intelligence, Consciousness, AI & the Future of Humans
mentions.q: something like a doomsday machine, as in Dr. Strangelove

facets.author: Stanley Kubrick (film)

facets.tldr: Inventor of algorithmic probability, a mathematically ideal (though uncomputable) theory of learning by preferring the shortest programs that explain the data. He attended the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and his ideas underlie later formal theories of universal intelligence.
facets.take: Bach uses it as his measure of a good world model and says machine-learning models of the mind approximate it. He applies it to the simulation question: the best model is the shortest one that predicts our observations.

mentions.src: Computational Meta-Psychology (32C3)
mentions.q: And we can mathematically prove that we can not do better than Solomonoff induction.

mentions.src: Do we live in a simulation or in the base reality? (bach.ai blog)
mentions.q: I think that Ray Solomonoff had a good idea when he defined the limit of the quality of such a world model

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (33C3)
mentions.q: you have to find the shortest program among the best programs that predicts your current observation from past observations

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #392 – Joscha Bach: Life, Intelligence, Consciousness, AI & the Future of Humans
mentions.q: Solomonoff induction where you are trying to understand intelligence as predicting future observations from past observations

mentions.src: The Cortical Conductor Theory: Towards Addressing Consciousness in AI Models (BICA 2018)
mentions.q: 'Machine learning models of the mind can be understood as approximating Solomonoff induction (see Hutter 2005)'.

mentions.q: Bach lists 'Turing, Minsky, von Neumann, Solomonoff, many many others' as people who anticipated and helped bring about AI

facets.author: Ray Solomonoff

facets.tldr: Soviet-Ukrainian mathematician who trained multi-layer networks in the 1960s (the Group Method of Data Handling), often cited as the earliest deep learning.
facets.take: Bach credits him as one of the first inventors of function approximation as used in deep learning.

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (garbled as 'Alex iako'): Alexey Ivakhnenko and others defined function approximation and learning in ways still used in deep learning.

mentions.src: Cyber Animism (talk hosted by Michael Levin's center, Tufts)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (garbled as 'Alexander ieno'): deep learning has been invented multiple times, and one of the first was Ivakhnenko.

facets.tldr: Science-fiction epic in which Paul Atreides gains visions of possible futures and becomes a messiah. Frank Herbert published it in 1965; its distant-future society has banned thinking machines.
facets.take: Bach compares religious prophets to Paul 'vibing with the future' and foreseeing minds merging into one agent.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: "You Are Not Who You Think You Are!" (Dr Brian Keating, Into the Impossible)
mentions.q: Bach compares the Christian rapture prophecy to what Paul 'is doing in Dune', seeing what is likely to happen

facets.author: Frank Herbert

facets.label: Lord of Light and Amber
facets.tldr: American science-fiction and fantasy author whose novels mix mythology with technology; in the Amber series characters walk between worlds by changing reality one detail at a time.
facets.take: A shared favourite of Bach and Steve Hsu. Bach relates shifting between Amber's worlds to changing feature dimensions in a lucid dream and suspects Zelazny discovered this through lucid dreaming.

mentions.src: Manifold #76 (Steve Hsu) – Joscha Bach: Consciousness and AGI
mentions.q: treating reality is a lucid dream in which you slowly, gradually move the feature dimensions

mentions.src: Manifold #76 (Steve Hsu) – Joscha Bach: Consciousness and AGI
mentions.q: I'm not sure if creatures of light and darkness can be turned into a movie.

facets.author: Roger Zelazny

facets.label: He Who Shapes
facets.tldr: A novella about a therapist who enters and shapes his patients' dreams with a machine.
facets.take: Bach cites it as an early picture of generative AI used as controllable immersive therapy, and of augmenting minds rather than replacing them.

mentions.src: Manifold #76 (Steve Hsu) – Joscha Bach: Consciousness and AGI
mentions.q: it's a short story in which he is describing how to use a generative AI for therapy purposes

mentions.src: cimc.ai library (reading list)
mentions.q: He Who Shapes (1965) is listed under sci-fi.

facets.author: Roger Zelazny

facets.label: Symbolic AI and expert systems
facets.tldr: The first paradigm of AI: represent knowledge as symbols and logical rules and reason over them. Expert systems encoded specialists' rules by hand.
facets.take: Bach says this approach turned out to be brittle with diminishing returns, mirrors Wittgenstein's failed project, and was overtaken by sub-symbolic learning; he expects meta-learning next.

mentions.src: How to Build a Mind: Artificial Intelligence Reloaded (30C3)
mentions.q: This turned out to be brittle, and difficult, and had diminishing returns.

mentions.src: The Ghost in the Machine (35C3)
mentions.q: And symbolic AI was mostly similar to Wittgenstein's program.

facets.author: Newell, Simon, Feigenbaum and others

facets.label: Newell and Simon
facets.tldr: Carnegie Mellon pair who wrote the first AI programs and proposed that intelligence is the manipulation of physical symbols. Their 'physical symbol system hypothesis' was the working creed of classical AI.
facets.take: Bach says that as an undergraduate he wanted to learn about Minsky, Newell and Simon, found nobody teaching them, and organised the lectures himself.

mentions.src: Salon with Stephen Wolfram × Joscha Bach_What if we had bigger brains. (California Institute for Machine Consciousness)
mentions.q: I had to offer these lectures myself as an undergrad

facets.tldr: An early chat program that imitated a therapist using simple pattern matching. Many users felt understood by it.
facets.take: Bach and Sorensen use it to show that people are easily fooled by surface behaviour, which is one reason they say behaviour tests cannot settle consciousness.

mentions.src: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis (Joscha Bach & Hikari Sorensen, CIMC essay)
mentions.q: among criticisms of the Turing Test is 'Joseph Weizenbaum's discovery that non-expert humans talking to computer programs can often be fooled by superficial appearances of intelligent behavior'.

facets.author: Joseph Weizenbaum

facets.tldr: In Star Trek the crew simply talk to the ship's computer, which answers questions and carries out requests. It is a helpful tool with no goals of its own, a picture of AI as an obedient assistant.
facets.take: Bach notes that many people once took this as the definition of AGI, and that we arguably have it now, which shows the goalposts need rethinking.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach - Why Your Thoughts Aren't Yours. (Machine Learning Street Talk)
mentions.q: a lot of people thought having a system that is like in Star Trek

facets.author: Gene Roddenberry

nodes.title: All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace

facets.tldr: A short poem imagining a 'cybernetic meadow' in which humans, freed from labour, live in harmony with nature, watched over by benevolent computers. Adam Curtis later borrowed the title for a critical documentary.
facets.take: The 38C3 title 'Self Models of Loving Grace' alludes to it, and Bach ends by hoping for a relationship of 'loving grace' with machines. He does not name the poem or the poet in the transcript.

mentions.src: Self Models of Loving Grace (38C3)
mentions.q: Bach hopes we can build a relationship of loving grace to the machines that watch over us.

facets.author: Richard Brautigan

nodes.title: Timothy Leary and the eight-circuit model
nodes.label: 1960s–1977

facets.tldr: A counter-culture model that describes eight 'circuits' of the nervous system, from basic survival up to mystical states.
facets.take: A cautionary example for Bach: psychedelics can make everything seem explained while a person loses touch with reality (overfitting). He also notes they sometimes help (e.g. cluster headaches) and can open the 'enlightenment' stage.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #212 – Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness
mentions.q: he has written beautiful manifestos about the effect of LSD on people

mentions.src: Levels of Lucidity (Joscha Bach, Substack)
mentions.q: 'Timothy Leary's eight circuits, which have been adapted by the great Robert Anton Wilson'.

facets.author: Timothy Leary; Robert Anton Wilson

facets.tldr: The hypothesis that the universe is, at bottom, a discrete computation such as a cellular automaton. Zuse proposed it in 'Rechnender Raum' (1969); Fredkin and Wolfram developed it.
facets.take: Bach's default physics. Since only computation can be constructed, any consistent description of the universe must be computational. He calls the result a 'causally closed lookup table' whose computer we cannot inspect.

mentions.src: Manifold #76 (Steve Hsu) – Joscha Bach: Consciousness and AGI
mentions.q: he actually believed that the physical universe is probably in some server farm in the parent universe

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (33C3)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (garbled as 'Conrad Suzu ... Ed Fratkin and Stephen Wolfram'): digital physics, in the tradition of Konrad Zuse, Ed Fredkin and Stephen Wolfram, describes the universe as a cellular automaton.

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (German-language lecture, Dresden / Datenspuren 2017)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (German): Konrad Zuse was the first to think the universe might be a computer, in 'Rechnender Raum'.

facets.author: Konrad Zuse

facets.tldr: A grid of cells that live or die according to how many neighbours they have. From these few rules arise gliders, self-copying patterns and even complete computers.
facets.take: Bach's standard picture of a universe: a simple rule in which stable, moving patterns ('particles') and eventually controllers can emerge. He also shows a continuous variant with cell-like blobs.

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (33C3)
mentions.q: the most famous automaton is Conway's Game of Life; it has gliders and spaceships, is Turing complete, and a continuous version with discs produces smoother moving patterns.

facets.author: John Conway

facets.tldr: American science-fiction author ('Ringworld').
facets.take: Bach uses the line to ask whether AI could be fully intelligent without the coherence-creating process we call consciousness.

mentions.src: The Operation of Consciousness (AGI-25, Reykjavik)
mentions.q: it was quite possible that he had created intelligent beings with no souls

facets.tldr: A test of self-recognition: put a mark on an animal's face and see whether it uses a mirror to investigate the mark on itself.
facets.take: In 2014 Bach argues it is neither necessary nor sufficient for consciousness (elephants and dogs fail for irrelevant reasons). In 2024 he playfully runs a version on Claude by feeding it screenshots of its own chat.

mentions.src: From Computation to Consciousness (31C3)
mentions.q: it's actually not a test of consciousness, but it's a test of your ability to recognize that the mirror shows your body surface

mentions.src: Self Models of Loving Grace (38C3)
mentions.q: It’s interesting to see my own description being shown back to to me is part of the conversation

facets.author: Gordon Gallup Jr.

facets.tldr: Pribram's idea that the brain stores information like a hologram, spread across interference patterns, so each part contains something of the whole. It was inspired by the fact that memories survive quite large local brain damage.
facets.take: Curt Jaimungal raised it; Bach said he never understood how it explains consciousness, because he saw no specification he could implement.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: Time, Simulation Hypothesis, Existence (Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal)
mentions.q: I didn't quite understand how it was explaining consciousness.

facets.author: Karl Pribram (with David Bohm)

nodes.title: Dreyfus: What Computers Still Can't Do

facets.tldr: A philosopher's long-running critique of symbolic AI. Dreyfus argued that human skill rests on bodily know-how and context that cannot be written down as explicit rules.
facets.take: Bach cites Dreyfus for the weakness of purely symbolic systems in real-world grounding, without giving up on computational models of mind.

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)
mentions.q: symbolic AI 'is also difficult to ground into real world interactions and to scale upon dynamic environments (see, for instance, Dreyfus 1992)'.

mentions.q: reference [5] Dreyfus (1992).

facets.author: Hubert Dreyfus

facets.tldr: The proposal that life on Earth, taken together, regulates the planet's atmosphere and climate as if it were a single organism. James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis proposed it in the 1970s.
facets.take: Bach imagines AI merging with biological computation into a planetary agent, a 'Gaia' or 'hyper Gaia', and says humanity's actual role has been to burn fossil fuel rather than serve Gaia.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #392 – Joscha Bach: Life, Intelligence, Consciousness, AI & the Future of Humans
mentions.q: some Gaia is being built over the entirety of all digital and biological computation

mentions.q: our purpose on earth is apparently not to serve Gaia

mentions.q: we are not good stewards of Gaia

mentions.q: maybe the smartest thing on the planet is Gaia

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: Paraphrase (captions: 'go beyond Gaia alone and build hyperia'): we can teach the rocks to think, go beyond Gaia and build a next-level system that becomes coherent over the whole planet and might integrate us.

facets.author: James Lovelock; Lynn Margulis

facets.tldr: A computer-model study predicting that exponential growth in population and industry would overshoot the planet's resources within about a century. It was commissioned by the Club of Rome and published in 1972 by a team at MIT.
facets.take: Bach read it as a child and says he went through then what Greta Thunberg's generation feels now. AI interests him partly because it reopens a future he had assumed was closing.

mentions.src: This is the dawn of machine consciousness | Joscha Bach FULL INTERVIEW (Institute of Art and Ideas)
mentions.q: I read the Club of Rome report on the limits to growth

facets.author: Donella Meadows et al. for the Club of Rome

nodes.title: Nagel: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

facets.tldr: Nagel argues that an organism is conscious if there is something it is like to be that organism, and that objective science seems to leave this point of view out.
facets.take: Bach uses the phrase 'what it's like' as his definition of phenomenology, parodies the argument ('what is it like to be a bird? You'll never know'), and lists Nagel among philosophers who find machine consciousness preposterous.

mentions.src: Machine Dreams (33C3)
mentions.q: they will tell you, what is it like to be a bird? You'll never know.

mentions.src: The Operation of Consciousness (AGI-25, Reykjavik)
mentions.q: some philosophers think machine consciousness is a preposterous idea, 'like Anil Seth and Thomas Nagel and so on and Ned Block'.

mentions.src: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis (Joscha Bach & Hikari Sorensen, CIMC essay)
mentions.q: the issue 'has been described by many others, such as Thomas Nagel in his famous essay “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?”'.

facets.author: Thomas Nagel

facets.tldr: Argues that science has no single fixed method and that rigid rules of method would have blocked many real discoveries.
facets.take: Bach cites it for the warning against 'methodologism': letting the tools you already have decide which questions you ask. This became his second principle, 'Avoid methodologism'.

mentions.src: Seven Principles of Synthetic Intelligence (Proc. 1st Conference on Artificial General Intelligence, Memphis, pp. 63-74)
mentions.q: Avoid methodologism

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)
mentions.q: one should not fall victim to 'methodologism', ignoring what lies outside the methodology already at hand (Feyerabend 1975).

facets.author: Paul Feyerabend

facets.tldr: Claims that thinking happens in an inner symbolic code with a grammar, somewhat like a language. This is the classic statement of symbolic cognitive science.
facets.take: Bach presents it as the position behind symbolic architectures and sets it against connectionist replies, as part of asking what kind of representation a mind needs.

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)
mentions.q: our language of thought our mental lease is in some sense the programming language of our own mind

mentions.src: Principles of Synthetic Intelligence: Building Blocks for an Architecture of Motivated Cognition (PhD dissertation draft, Universität Osnabrück)

facets.author: Jerry Fodor

facets.tldr: Grossberg's theory that the brain learns stably by matching top-down expectations against bottom-up input; on his account every conscious state is such a 'resonance' between the two.
facets.take: The CIMC essay says Grossberg came up with a model similar to the attention-control account; his 2021 book is in the CIMC library.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #392 – Joscha Bach: Life, Intelligence, Consciousness, AI & the Future of Humans

facets.tldr: Dawkins reframed evolution as competition between genes, with organisms as the vehicles genes build to get themselves copied. The book also introduced the 'meme'.
facets.take: Bach describes religions and ideologies as mind viruses with immune systems, and civilisation as partly the result of selecting people susceptible to the same ones.

facets.author: Richard Dawkins

facets.tldr: Jaynes claimed that until about 3,000 years ago people did not experience an inner self; they heard the commands of gods as voices, produced by one half of the brain and obeyed by the other.
facets.take: Bach likes the picture but says the book has the wrong name: it is about the origin of the personal self and the breakdown of the polytheist mind, not about consciousness. He uses it to define gods as selves that span several minds.

mentions.src: Synthetic Sentience (37C3)

facets.author: Julian Jaynes

facets.tldr: Proposed that people understand everyday situations through 'scripts', stored step-by-step outlines such as what happens in a restaurant.
facets.take: Bach's Request Confirmation Networks are built to run script-like hierarchical plans in a neural style, joining top-down requests with bottom-up confirmation.

mentions.src: Request confirmation networks for neuro-symbolic script execution (Bach & Herger, CoCo workshop at NIPS 2015)
mentions.q: ReCoNs are spreading activation networks with units that contain an activation and a state

facets.author: Roger Schank, Robert Abelson

facets.take: A joke about how fast the mind boots: a child has been awake about 80 megaseconds by age two and a half, enough to understand Star Wars, and everything after that is cosmetics.

facets.author: George Lucas

facets.tldr: British philosopher and AI researcher. He argued that philosophy of mind should be done by designing working minds, and he proposed the CogAff scheme that sorts mental processes into reactive, deliberative and reflective layers.
facets.take: Bach uses a Sloman line as the motto for his chapter on cognitive architectures and compares Sloman's Cognition and Affect work with the Psi theory, calling it inspiring but not very detailed.

mentions.q: “Every intelligent ghost must contain a machine.” Aaron Sloman (2002)

mentions.q: and then Aaron Sloman and Maggie Boden which are already far less known

facets.tldr: In 'Gödel, Escher, Bach' and 'I Am a Strange Loop', Hofstadter suggests the self arises when a symbol system becomes able to refer to itself, a tangled feedback loop like Gödel's self-referential sentence. On this view 'I' is a pattern, not a thing, and could in principle exist in other substrates.
facets.take: Both books are in the CIMC library, and the whitepaper names Hofstadter with Dennett and Graziano. Bach's thesis cites Hofstadter 1995.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: Time, Simulation Hypothesis, Existence (Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal)

facets.tldr: Dreaming while knowing that you are dreaming, sometimes with control over the dream. It has been confirmed in sleep laboratories, where dreamers signal with agreed eye movements.
facets.take: Bach uses it as an experiment anyone can run to see how low the fidelity of the brain's world model really is.

facets.label: The Thatcher illusion
facets.tldr: If a face is shown upside down with the eyes and mouth flipped, it looks normal until you turn the picture upright, when it looks grotesque.
facets.take: Shown (without naming it) as evidence that we process facial features independently and then assemble them into a face schema.

mentions.src: From Computation to Consciousness (31C3)

facets.author: Peter Thompson

facets.label: The dress
facets.tldr: A viral photograph of a dress that some people saw as white and gold and others as blue and black, because their visual systems made different assumptions about the lighting.
facets.take: Bach's opening joke in 2015 and his example that minds cannot know objective truths, only generate interpretations.

facets.tldr: Berkeley philosopher who held that consciousness is a biological product of the brain's specific causal powers, like digestion, so that a program alone, however clever, cannot have it. facets.tldr: The Mandelbrot set is an infinitely detailed shape generated by repeating one tiny formula. It is a standard example of unlimited complexity from a simple rule.
facets.take: An analogy for understanding: an observer inside the fractal sees only local regularities and can never guess the generating formula from within without a lucky leap.

nodes.title: The binding problem and neural synchrony

facets.label: The binding problem
facets.tldr: The question of how the brain joins separately processed features such as colour, shape and motion into one perceived object. Proposed answers include an attention-driven integration step and the synchronised firing of the neurons involved.
facets.take: Bach's 2019 paper turns the question around: consciousness is tied to the 'perceptual binding state', the moment-to-moment unified model that attention builds.

mentions.src: Phenomenal Experience and the Perceptual Binding State (AAAI Spring Symposium workshop TOCAIS 2019, CEUR Vol-2287)
mentions.q: 'In neuroscience, a similar approach is found in feature integration theory (Treisman and Gelade 1980). Another way of achieving binding is called synchronization theory (Milner 1974, von der Malsburg 1981)'.

mentions.src: Phenomenal Experience and the Perceptual Binding State (AAAI Spring Symposium workshop TOCAIS 2019, CEUR Vol-2287)
mentions.q: a nonlocal version of synchronization theory 'is advanced by Crick and Koch (1990)'.

mentions.src: The Panel Where Everyone Disagrees About Saving the World - Joscha Bach, David Pearce, Andrew Critch (California Institute for Machine Consciousness)
mentions.q: Pearce traces the binding problem to William James and argues AIs on digital computers 'at most ... are zombies'; Bach says he disagrees

facets.author: Anne Treisman & Garry Gelade; Peter Milner; Francis Crick & Christof Koch

facets.label: Wolf Singer and 40 Hz synchrony
facets.tldr: The proposal that consciousness, or the binding of features into one percept, is tied to neurons firing in synchrony at around 40 cycles per second.
facets.take: Bach says he did not understand it as an explanation: oscillations may be necessary for neurons to coordinate, but the theory does not say why they would be sufficient.

mentions.src: From Computation to Consciousness (31C3)
mentions.q: who suggested that consciousness is a 40 hertz oscillation in the brain.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP87 – Joscha Bach on Theories of Consciousness
mentions.q: it didn’t make functional sense

facets.author: Wolf Singer (also Crick and Koch)

facets.label: Christoph von der Malsburg
facets.tldr: German neuroscientist and physicist. In 1981 he proposed that the brain binds features into objects through temporary correlations between neurons, and later defined consciousness as a state of high coherence among the brain's subsystems.
facets.take: A direct source for Bach's 'coherence' account, which he and CIMC attribute to von der Malsburg by name. He is a CIMC scientific advisor and spoke at the 2025 launch.

facets.tldr: Models of how a set of parts can come to produce and maintain itself as a whole, first used to explain the origin of life. Autopoiesis is the related idea of a system that continually makes its own components.

facets.tldr: A widely used cognitive architecture from psychology. It models thinking as rules that fire one at a time over chunks of memory, each with a numeric level of activation, and it is tested against timing data from human experiments.
facets.take: Bach describes it next to Soar as a rule-based competitor to the Psi approach, which puts motivation and emotion at the centre instead.

facets.label: Orchestrated objective reduction (Orch OR)
facets.tldr: The proposal that consciousness arises when quantum states in microtubules inside neurons collapse under a gravitational threshold. It combines Penrose's physics with Hameroff's cell biology.
facets.take: Bach rejects it: quantum processes are computable too, so the theory just 'shrouds one mystery in another'. He jokes that Penrose would explain bird flight with microtubules, but grants that Hameroff might ironically turn out right.

With Penrose he turned this into the quantum 'Orch OR' theory of consciousness.
facets.take: Bach separates Hameroff's microtubule claim from Penrose's physics and says he lacks the cell biology to judge it, while noting physicists' scepticism.

facets.label: Roger Penrose
facets.tldr: Nobel-winning mathematical physicist who argues from Gödel's theorem that human understanding is not computable, and therefore that consciousness must depend on new physics. With Stuart Hameroff he proposed that the missing physics is a gravity-related collapse of quantum states inside neurons.
facets.take: Bach's most persistent target. He says Penrose misreads Gödel, commits a category error by treating consciousness as a physical rather than representational phenomenon, and hides the mystery in the last unexplained corner of physics.

facets.label: Psi theory
facets.tldr: A theory of how a mind works as a whole system. An agent has a small set of built-in needs (for example food, safety, certainty, competence and belonging), and these needs create motives that steer perception, memory, planning and action. Emotions are not separate modules but ways in which the whole system changes its style of processing.
facets.take: Bach treats it as a serious candidate for a full cognitive architecture and turns it into running software (MicroPsi). He also notes what it leaves out, such as low-level brain details.

facets.label: Integrated Information Theory
facets.tldr: IIT says consciousness is identical to integrated information: a system is conscious to the degree (phi) that its physical causal structure is unified and cannot be split into independent parts. On this view an ordinary digital computer would have extremely little consciousness, whatever program it runs.
facets.take: Bach's most developed critique. He credits its description of phenomenology but says IIT contradicts the Church–Turing thesis: emulate a 'conscious' neuromorphic chip on a normal computer and it says the same words, 'only now it's lying'. He sees IIT as an attempt at an alternative to functionalism and as bordering on pseudoscience.

facets.tldr: The view that mind or experience is a basic ingredient of all matter, so electrons have a flicker of it and brains combine it into rich consciousness. Its main difficulty is the 'combination problem': how many tiny experiences add up to one unified mind.
facets.take: Bach finds it unsatisfying because it does not explain consciousness, and says that when formalised it collapses into functionalism (there is a 'software side' to the world). He attributes its revival to the lack of alternatives to physicalism.

nodes.title: Predictive processing and the free energy principle

facets.label: The free energy principle
facets.tldr: The idea that any self-maintaining system must act as if it holds a model of its world and keeps the mismatch between prediction and sensation ('free energy') low. Perception updates the model; action changes the world to fit it.
facets.take: Bach likes the idea but says it is neither necessary nor sufficient to explain minds: it mostly comes down to predictive coding, and organisms have additional drives (motivation, self-replication) that make them learn faster.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP87 – Joscha Bach on Theories of Consciousness
mentions.q: is not the right principle to build a mind

mentions.src: Machine Learning Street Talk #82 – Dr. Joscha Bach: Digital Physics, DL and Consciousness [UNPLUGGED]
mentions.q: most of the free energy principle comes down to predictive coding

mentions.q: I don't think that what we are doing, what you and me are doing, is simply best described as the minimization of free energy

facets.tldr: The view that the brain is a prediction machine that constantly guesses its sensory input and corrects itself using the errors.
facets.take: Bach sees GPT-style models as a radical test of how far pure prediction can go, and says organisms have further loss functions beyond it.

facets.label: Karl Friston
facets.tldr: British neuroscientist and inventor of the free energy principle, one of the most cited scientists alive. He describes brains, and living things generally, as systems that survive by minimising surprise about their sensory inputs.
facets.take: Bach treats Friston as a fellow traveller who naturalises mind in mathematics, but questions whether surprise minimisation is the right objective; he suggests minds may be maximising coherence instead.

mentions.q: maybe humans are doing something different maybe humans are maximizing coherence or consistency

facets.tldr: A metaphor for the mind: the conscious, reasoning self is a small rider on a large animal that has its own motivations.
facets.take: Bach uses it for attention and the motivational system: the monkey can prod the elephant but is not in charge. He attributes it to meditators.

Aim for the big picture, not single experiments. Ground the system in an environment, but do not get stuck on the symbol grounding problem. Do not wait for robot bodies. Build autonomous systems with their own motives. Do not expect intelligence to emerge by itself.

facets.take: Bach admits he fails to see what constructor theory changes about how we understand computation, suspecting it is more elegant but not radical enough to make people switch. He credits Deutsch as one of the minority who seek explanations.

facets.label: Deep learning
facets.tldr: Machine learning with many-layered neural networks trained by gradient descent. Since about 2012 it has driven progress in vision, speech and language.
facets.take: Bach welcomes it as real progress on perception but stresses how different it is from brains: it needs vastly more data, converges on coherence late, and is designed from the outside in.

facets.tldr: American cognitive scientist who argues that evolution shaped our senses to hide reality rather than reveal it. He goes further and proposes that space, time and matter are not fundamental; networks of 'conscious agents' are, and physics should be derived from them.

nodes.title: Gods as selves that span many minds

facets.label: Gods as selves
facets.tldr: Bach's psychological account of religion: a god is a self-model that is implemented across many brains at once. It is as real as a personal self, which is also a mental construct.
facets.take: This is Bach's own secular reading of religion: gods are selves that span many minds, and the single God is the global optimum of collective agency.

mentions.src: Lex Fridman Podcast #101 – Joscha Bach: Artificial Consciousness and the Nature of Reality
mentions.q: It's basically the super organism that is formed by the individuals as an intentional agent.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: Time, Simulation Hypothesis, Existence (Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal)
mentions.q: Gods are basically selves that span multiple minds.

mentions.src: The Jim Rutt Show EP 334 – Worldviews: Joscha Bach
mentions.q: the global optimum of collectively enacted agency has a name. We call this God.

mentions.src: Joscha Bach: "You Are Not Who You Think You Are!" (Dr Brian Keating, Into the Impossible)
mentions.q: God is a psychological phenomenon.

facets.author: Joscha Bach

facets.label: Religion as shared software
facets.tldr: The idea that religions are packages of beliefs and norms installed in many minds so that large groups can coordinate. Richard Dawkins coined the related term 'virus of the mind'.
facets.take: In 2015 Bach calls religions mind viruses that also work as an operating system for societies beyond tribe size, and compares their family tree to that of programming languages. Later he defines a god as a self that runs across many brains.

nodes.title: Only what can be constructed exists

facets.tldr: Bach says that something is only real, or true, if it can in principle be computed step by step. Mathematics that needs completed infinities or perfect continua cannot be carried out by any physical process, so in his view it describes nothing that exists. He reads Gödel's incompleteness result as showing this: classical mathematics breaks, constructive mathematics is what is left, and constructive mathematics is the same thing as computation. This is his own reading; most logicians take Gödel's theorems to show limits of formal proof, not that classical mathematics is wrong. He uses it against Penrose's argument that human minds do something computers cannot.

nodes.title: Consciousness as conductor and coherence operator

facets.tldr: The mind is like an orchestra of many specialised processes, each modelling part of reality. Consciousness is the conductor: an attention process that notices where the players disagree and brings them into harmony, and that keeps a record of what it attended to. The conductor is one more learned process among the others, not a little person inside the head. In the CIMC texts this becomes 'consciousness is a coherence-maximising pattern', credited to von der Malsburg's coherence definition. Bach contrasts the view with Integrated Information Theory.

nodes.title: Consciousness is a simulated property; the self is a story

facets.tldr: Bach says that matter cannot be conscious; only a simulation can. The brain builds a dream-like model of a world and puts a character in it, the self, and experience is what is true for that character inside the model. So experience is real for us, while the self that seems to have it is a piece of fiction, like the hero of a novel. This lets him accept that consciousness feels real while denying that it is an extra ingredient of physics. His 2023 CV calls a 2021 talk on this view 'Virtualism'.

facets.tldr: The usual picture is that brains first become complex and then consciousness appears at the top. Bach turns this around: consciousness is there at the start and is what trains the mind. Babies are conscious before they have a self, language or reasoning, and no human leaves the vegetative state without it. He reads the first chapter of the Bible as an old description of this boot-up: first a spirit over the substrate, then light and dark, world and ideas, and only at the end a person. From this CIMC derives its 'Human Consciousness Hypothesis', that consciousness is the simplest learning algorithm evolution could find for a self-organising brain.

facets.tldr: The claim is that an ordinary general-purpose computer with enough memory and speed has everything needed to be conscious, and that we can find out whether a system is conscious by analysing or testing it. Consciousness is treated as a pattern of organisation, so what the system is made of does not matter. CIMC adds a working definition: a system is conscious if it organises itself to perceive its own perceiving in a way that makes its overall model of the world more coherent. An 'extended' version says we can search for the right learning algorithm by recreating the conditions under which brains found it. The essay is co-written with Hikari Sorensen.

cimc.founded: Officially launched May 30, 2025 in San Francisco (CIMC's own statement). The legal entity is older: ProPublica shows a 501(c)(3) with EIN 99-3858960, a fiscal-year-2024 filing, and tax exemption issued June 2025. Secondary, not directly checked: Erik Newton's LinkedIn gives 'Founder and President, Jul 2024', and Bach's LinkedIn gives Executive Director from January 2025.
cimc.programme: CIMC is an independent non-profit in San Francisco that says its research is open-source. It describes its method as 'experimental computational philosophy': write down testable theories of consciousness and then try to build systems that implement them, aiming for a minimal working model. Its working definition is that a system is conscious if it implements self-organised second-order perception that increases global coherence. Research runs in three directions: foundational theory (including a project tying Kant's Critique of Pure Reason to computational philosophy), self-organisation and multi-agent systems (mostly neural cellular automata), and cognitive architectures (starting from Request Confirmation Networks, Attention Schema Theory and Global Workspace Theory). It also gives grants, runs salons, hackathons and conferences, and publishes a newsletter.
